title: there ... and it ...
subtitle: There's a new restaurant. It's very good.
summary: Use there to say that something exists (there is / there was / there will be), and it to talk about a particular thing, place, fact or situation.

lesson.heading: there ... = something exists
lesson.text: We use **there ...** when we mention something for the first time, to say that it exists. *'**There's** a new restaurant in Hill Street.' 'Yes, I know. I've heard **it's** very good.'*

examples.text: **There's** a new restaurant in Hill Street.
I'm sorry I'm late. **There was** a lot of traffic.
examples.wrong: It was a lot of traffic

examples.text: Things are very expensive now. **There has been** a big rise in the cost of living.

lesson.heading: there or it?

left.label: there
left.text: Something exists - we are mentioning it for the first time.
examples: The house is unoccupied. **There's** nobody living **there**.

right.label: it
right.text: A particular thing, place, fact or situation that we already know about.
examples: We went to the new restaurant. **It's** very good.
I wasn't expecting her to call me. **It was** a complete surprise.

lesson.note: Compare in one sentence: I like this town. **There's** a lot to do here. **It's** an interesting place.

lesson.heading: there + will be / must be / used to be ...
lesson.text: You can use **there** with will, must, might, should, going to, used to and with sure to / bound to / likely to / supposed to.

examples.text: 'Is there a flight to Rome tonight?' '**There might be**. I'll check online.'
If people drove more carefully, **there wouldn't be** so many accidents.
I could hear music coming from the house. **There must have been** somebody at home.
**There's bound to be** a cafe somewhere near here.

lesson.heading: there and it in the same structures
lesson.text: Keep **there** for the thing that exists and **it** for the particular thing you are talking about.

examples.text: They live on a busy road. **There must be** a lot of noise from the traffic.
They live on a busy road. **It must be** very noisy.
examples.note: it = living on a busy road

examples.text: **There used to be** a cinema here, but it closed a few years ago.
That building is now a supermarket. **It used to be** a cinema.
There's a flight to Rome tonight, but **it's** sure to be full.

lesson.heading: It's dangerous to ...
lesson.text: We normally begin sentences like this with **It**, not with the whole to-phrase.

examples.text: **It's dangerous to walk** in the road.
examples.wrong: To walk in the road is dangerous

examples.text: **It didn't take** us long to get here.
**It's a shame** (that) you can't come to the party.
**It's not worth** waiting any longer. Let's go.

lesson.heading: it for distance, time and weather
lesson.text: We also use **it** to talk about distance, time and the weather.

examples.text: How far is **it** from here to the airport?
**It's** a long time since we last saw you.
**It was** windy. but **There was** a cold wind.

lesson.text: If the sentence introduces something new (a bridge, a reason, a car park), start with there; if it describes something already known, start with it.

exercises.prompt: The journey took a long time. ___ a lot of traffic.
exercises.explanation: We are saying that traffic existed, so we use there was (not it was).

exercises.prompt: ___ something wrong with the washing machine. It's not working properly.
exercises.explanation: We mention the problem for the first time, so we use there is.

exercises.prompt: I wanted to visit the museum yesterday, but ___ enough time.
exercises.explanation: Time did not exist for me, so the negative is there wasn't.

exercises.prompt: I can't find my phone. ___ in my bag - I just looked.
exercises.explanation: We are talking about one particular thing, the phone, so we use it.

exercises.prompt: How can we get across the river? ___ a bridge?
exercises.explanation: We are asking whether a bridge exists: Is there ... ?

exercises.prompt: I couldn't see anything. ___ completely dark.
exercises.explanation: It describes the situation, so we say It was completely dark.

exercises.prompt: About 50 people came to the meeting. Say the same thing beginning with There.
exercises.answer: There were about 50 people at the meeting
exercises.explanation: There + plural verb tells us how many people existed at the meeting.

exercises.prompt: There isn't a school in the village now. ___ one, but it closed a few years ago.
exercises.explanation: There used to be = a school existed in the past but does not exist now.

exercises.prompt: If people drove more carefully, ___ fewer accidents.
exercises.explanation: There can be used with would, will, might, must etc.: there would be.

exercises.statement: It's a long way from my house to the nearest shop.
exercises.explanation: Correct. We use it for distance.

exercises.statement: After the lecture it will be an opportunity to ask questions.
exercises.explanation: After the lecture there will be an opportunity to ask questions. The opportunity is something that will exist.

exercises.prompt: Does each sentence need there or it in the gap (shown as ...)?

items.text: Why was she so unfriendly? ... must have been a reason.
... 's a long time since we last saw you.
... used to be a lot of tourists here, but not many come now.
My phone won't work here. ... 's no signal.
... didn't take us long to get here.
We won't have any problem parking. ... 's sure to be a car park somewhere.
I'm sorry about what happened. ... was my fault.
